title: Cap. III Rat. 12: efficacious election from mere good pleasure destroys free choice
latin: Rat. 12. Si ponamus Deum efficaciter eligere quosdam ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praescientia meritorum, tolletur plane liberum arbitrium. Nam cum nemo potest resistere efficaci voluntati Dei, non manebit in eorum libera potestate gloriam amittere, qui hoc modo sunt ad gloriam praedestinati. Posita itaque tali antecedente voluntate Dei de salute Petri et Pauli, aut erit in illis absoluta necessitas operandi ea quae sunt necessaria ad salutem, puta credendi, pie vivendi, in fide et pietate perseverandi, atque adeo perveniendi ad ipsam salutem, aut Dei decretum efficax potest fieri irritum. Utrumque absurdum et impossibile. Ergo non debemus ponere electionem aliquorum efficacem ad gloriam, nisi ex praescientia meritorum quae orientur ex libero arbitrio per gratiam Dei praevento.
pass_a: Reason 12. If we posit that God efficaciously elects certain ones to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will, and not from foresight of merits, free choice will plainly be taken away. For since no one can resist the efficacious will of God, it will not remain in their free power to lose glory, who in this manner are predestined to glory. Such an antecedent will of God concerning the salvation of Peter and Paul having therefore been posited, either there will be in them an absolute necessity of doing those things which are necessary to salvation, for example of believing, of living piously, of persevering in faith and piety, and so of arriving at salvation itself, or the efficacious decree of God can be made void. Both absurd and impossible. Therefore we ought not to posit an efficacious election of some to glory, except from foresight of merits which will arise from free choice prevented by the grace of God.
pass_b: Rat. 12. If God efficaciously elects some to glory from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of merits, free choice is plainly destroyed. No one can resist God's efficacious will — so those so predestined to glory will not keep free power to lose it. Posit that antecedent will for the salvation of Peter and Paul: either they are under absolute necessity to do what salvation requires (believe, live piously, persevere in faith and piety, and so arrive at salvation), or God's efficacious decree can be made void. Both absurd and impossible. Therefore we must not posit efficacious election of some to glory except from foresight of merits that will arise from free choice preceded by God's grace.

lemmas.gloss: efficacious election from mere good pleasure

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: old Pelagian cantilena — Prosper, Faustus, Augustine's defense loci
latin: Sol. Antiqua fuit Pelagianorum cantilena, eos fatum inducere et liberum arbitrium perimere, qui statuunt absolutam et efficacem certorum hominum praedestinationem ante praescientiam meritorum. Id videre licet apud Prosperum, qui scribit Pelagianos infamasse Augustinum, dicentes Eum liberum arbitrium penitus submovere, et sub gratiae nomine necessitatem praedicare fatalem, De lib. arbit. pag. 223. Eadem objectio occurrit etiam in Responsionibus ejusdem ad capitula Gallorum Obj. 6. Porro Faustus Regiensis Semipelagianorum coryphaeus oblique perstringit Augustinum, et appellat liberi arbitrii interemtorem, qui omnia alterutram partem ex praedestinatione statuta et definita esse pronunciat, De lib. arbit. lib. 1. sect. 11. Atque dicit sub gratiae vocabulum absconditum esse ab illo fatale decretum, ibidem. Postremo, ipse Augustinus multis in locis cogitur hanc iniquissimam calumniam eluere: Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. et De bono persever. lib. 2. cap. 12. et alibi passim. Haec praemittere volui responsioni nostrae, ut ex quorum lacunis omnia fere adversariorum argumenta hauriantur intelligatis.
pass_a: Solution. It was an ancient ditty of the Pelagians, that those induce fate and destroy free choice who establish an absolute and efficacious predestination of certain human beings before foresight of merits. That may be seen in Prosper, who writes that the Pelagians defamed Augustine, saying that He utterly removes free choice, and under the name of grace preaches a fatal necessity, On free choice p. 223. The same objection occurs also in his Responses to the chapters of the Gauls Obj. 6. Further Faustus of Riez, coryphaeus of the Semipelagians, obliquely wounds Augustine, and calls him the destroyer of free choice, who pronounces all things on either side to be established and defined from predestination, On free choice book 1 section 11. And he says that under the word of grace a fatal decree is hidden by him, in the same place. Finally, Augustine himself in many places is compelled to wash away this most unfair calumny: Against the two Epistles of the Pelagians book 2 chapter 7, and On the Good of Perseverance book 2 chapter 12, and elsewhere everywhere. These things I wished to premise to our answer, that you may understand from whose pools nearly all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.
pass_b: Sol. An old Pelagian refrain: those who hold absolute, efficacious predestination of certain people before foresight of merits induce fate and destroy free choice. Prosper records Pelagians defaming Augustine as utterly removing free choice and preaching fatal necessity under the name of grace (De lib. arb. p. 223). The same charge is in his Responses to the Gallic chapters, Obj. 6. Faustus of Riez, Semipelagian champion, obliquely strikes Augustine as destroyer of free choice for saying everything on either side is fixed by predestination (De lib. arb. 1.11), and claims a fatal decree is hidden under the word grace. Augustine himself must often wash off that foul calumny (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; De bono persever. 2.12; and elsewhere). I premise this so you see from whose cisterns almost all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.

lemmas.gloss: old charge: fate and free choice destroyed

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: antecedent will to save does not coerce — free-moving means
latin: Jam ad rem. Nego posita antecedente Dei voluntate de danda Petro aeterna salute, tolli aut impediri liberum ejus arbitrium circa salutis consecutionem: et tamen illud simul assero, non posse illum, posita hac hypothesi, a salute excidere, ac per consequens, Divinum decretum non posse fieri irritum. Quod ad prius; Efficax Dei voluntas non modo operatur omnia quae vult Deus, sed eo modo, et per illa media quae vult. Ex efficaci igitur et antecedente proposito salvandi Petrum, non tenetur Deus uti mediis coactivis, aut necessitantibus voluntatem humanam, sed sufficit ut utatur illis, quae sapientia Divina novit efficaciter, infallibiliter, et tamen libere posse movere, et flectere ejus voluntatem. Imo et hoc etiam addo, Dum Deus ex antecedente decreto dandae salutis movet liberum arbitrium electorum ad salutem acquirendam, tantum abest ut inde amittatur, ut potius augeatur et roboretur humanae voluntatis libertas. Nam ut optime Bannes, In 1. qu. 22. art. 4, Liberum creaturae arbitrium accipit libertatem participatam ex Divino libero arbitrio, movente illud fortiter et suaviter juxta modum suae naturae.
pass_a: Now to the matter. I deny that, the antecedent will of God concerning giving eternal salvation to Peter having been posited, his free choice concerning the obtaining of salvation is taken away or hindered: and yet at the same time I assert that, this hypothesis having been posited, he cannot fall from salvation, and consequently, the Divine decree cannot be made void. As to the former; The efficacious will of God not only works all things which God wills, but in that manner, and through those means which he wills. From an efficacious and antecedent purpose therefore of saving Peter, God is not bound to use coercive means, or means necessitating the human will, but it suffices that he use those which the Divine wisdom knows can efficaciously, infallibly, and yet freely move and bend his will. Nay I also add this: While God from the antecedent decree of giving salvation moves the free choice of the elect toward acquiring salvation, so far is it from being lost thence, that rather the liberty of the human will is increased and strengthened. For as Báñez excellently, On 1. q. 22 art. 4, The free choice of the creature receives a participated liberty from the Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to the mode of its nature.
pass_b: Now to the point. I deny that God's antecedent will to give Peter eternal salvation takes away or hinders his free choice about obtaining it — and yet I affirm that, on that hypothesis, he cannot fall from salvation, so the divine decree cannot be made void. First: God's efficacious will works all he wills, but in the manner and by the means he wills. From an efficacious, antecedent purpose to save Peter he need not use coercive means that necessitate the human will; it is enough to use those Divine wisdom knows can move and bend the will efficaciously, infallibly, yet freely. Indeed, when from the antecedent decree to give salvation God moves the elect's free choice toward acquiring it, liberty is not lost but rather increased and strengthened. As Báñez puts it (In 1. q.22 a.4): the creature's free choice receives participated liberty from Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to its nature.

lemmas.gloss: deny free choice is taken away
non-coercive means that freely move the will
Báñez: strongly and sweetly according to nature

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: Augustine — God inclines hearts; elect act freely by inspired willing
latin: Sed Augustinum audiamus: Cum Deus vult fieri aliquid, quod non nisi volentibus hominibus oportet fieri, inclinantur eorum corda ut hoc velint eo inclinante, qui in nobis mirabili modo et ineffabili operatur et velle, De praed. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 20. Falsum ergo fuit illud prius assumptum Jesuitae, Posita, scilicet efficaci voluntate Divina de salute electorum, eos necessario, et non libere velle ac facere ea per quae perducuntur ad salutem: libere enim agunt, quia ut sic agant, ipse Deus inspirat illis liberrimum velle.
pass_a: But let us hear Augustine: When God wills something to be done, which ought to be done only by willing human beings, their hearts are inclined that they will this, he inclining who works in us in a wonderful and ineffable manner even to will, On the Predestination of the Saints book 1 chapter 20. False therefore was that prior assumption of the Jesuit, namely, The efficacious divine will concerning the salvation of the elect having been posited, that they necessarily, and not freely, will and do those things through which they are brought to salvation: for they act freely, because that they may so act, God himself inspires in them a most free willing.
pass_b: Hear Augustine: when God wills something that must be done only by willing people, their hearts are inclined to will it by him who works in us, wonderfully and ineffably, even the willing (De praed. Sanct. 1.20). So the Jesuit's first assumption was false — that once God's efficacious will for the elect's salvation is posited, they necessarily and not freely will and do what brings them to salvation. They act freely, because God himself inspires in them a most free willing so to act.

lemmas.gloss: God inclines hearts and works willing
elect will and act freely, not by necessity

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: can the elect fall? fragility vs maintaining hand of God — Peter
latin: Accedo ad illud posterius dictum Jesuitae, nimirum, Posse electum a salute excidere, et decretum Dei irritum fieri, si modo dicamus post efficax Dei decretum electos libere operari ad consecutionem salutis. Nam qui libere perseverat, potest non perseverare; potest ergo non salvari, et sic sequetur quod est impossibile, decretum Dei irritum reddi posse. Respondeo, Haec pronunciata, Qui libere operatur, potest non operari; Qui libere salvatur, potest non salvari; unde infertur decretum Dei efficax posse fieri irritum: haec, inquam, pronunciata, si respiciant possibilitatem non operandi, et non perveniendi ad salutem, quatenus ex humana fragilitate per se considerata nasci et oriri possit, agnoscimus ipsis electis adhaerescere talem pereundi, et a vita aeterna excidendi possibilitatem: Sed si referantur ad possibilitatem non operandi aut pereundi, quasi, non obstante manutinentia Divina, possit haec imbecillitas electorum in actum exire, atque sic eos quoad eventum posse non perseverare in fide et sanctitate, posse non pervenire ad vitam aeternam, negamus prorsus, posito decreto Dei efficaci de illorum salute, talem possibilitatem pereundi illis competere. Exemplo Petri hoc declaravit Augustinus; Potuit ille, ut homo infirmus et mutabilis, a fide et sanctitate et a salute deficere: sed hoc posito, quod Deus decreverat illi propter Christi orationem inspirare liberrimam, fortissimam, invictissimam, perseverantissimam in fide voluntatem, ex hac hypothesi non potuit perire, non potuit non liberrime perseverare; Vide De corr. et grat. c. 8.
pass_a: I come to that later saying of the Jesuit, namely, That the elect can fall from salvation, and the decree of God be made void, if only we say that after the efficacious decree of God the elect freely operate toward the obtaining of salvation. For he who freely perseveres can not persevere; he can therefore not be saved, and so there will follow what is impossible, that the decree of God can be rendered void. I answer, These pronouncements, He who freely operates can not operate; He who is freely saved can not be saved; whence it is inferred that the efficacious decree of God can be made void: these pronouncements, I say, if they look to the possibility of not operating, and of not arriving at salvation, inasmuch as it can be born and arise from human fragility considered in itself, we acknowledge that such a possibility of perishing, and of falling from eternal life, adheres to the elect themselves: But if they are referred to the possibility of not operating or of perishing, as if, the Divine upholding not withstanding, this weakness of the elect could go forth into act, and so that as to the event they could not persevere in faith and holiness, could not arrive at eternal life, we deny altogether that, the efficacious decree of God concerning their salvation having been posited, such a possibility of perishing belongs to them. By the example of Peter Augustine declared this; He could, as a weak and changeable human being, fall from faith and holiness and from salvation: but this having been posited, that God had decreed to inspire in him on account of Christ's prayer a most free, most strong, most unconquered, most persevering will in the faith, from this hypothesis he could not perish, he could not but most freely persevere; See On Rebuke and Grace chapter 8.
pass_b: Next the Jesuit's later claim: if after God's efficacious decree the elect freely work toward salvation, an elect person can fall from salvation and God's decree can be made void — for whoever freely perseveres can fail to persevere, so can fail to be saved. I answer: the sayings Whoever freely acts can fail to act and Whoever is freely saved can fail to be saved, if they mean a possibility of not acting and not reaching salvation that can arise from human fragility considered in itself, we grant such a possibility of perishing still clings to the elect. But if they mean that, despite God's upholding hand, that weakness can go into act so that in the event they might not persevere in faith and holiness or reach eternal life — we deny entirely that, once God's efficacious decree for their salvation is posited, such a possibility of perishing belongs to them. Augustine shows it by Peter (De corr. et grat. 8): as a weak, changeable man he could fall from faith, holiness, and salvation — but given that God had decreed, for Christ's prayer, to inspire in him a most free, strong, unconquered, persevering will in the faith, on that hypothesis he could not perish and could not but most freely persevere.

lemmas.gloss: Jesuit: free perseverance implies possible failure
fragility in itself vs God's upholding

lemmas.lemma: Petrus / De corr. et grat. c. 8

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12 close: God's hand leads firmly and sweetly — Valentia, Catharinus
latin: Manus igitur Dei est, non nostra, ut non discedamus a Deo: Manus autem Dei tanta efficacitate ducit et dirigit electos ad vitam aeternam, ut inde firmissimum stet ejus decretum; et simul tanta suavitate et libertate, ut inde liberrimum in bono fiat illorum arbitrium. Haec simul constare posse, fatetur Valentia, In 1. qu. 23. disp. 1. puncto 4. ubi ostendit, antiquissimos et doctissimos Scholasticos in hac opinione fuisse constitutos. Ambrosius etiam Catharinus affirmat, concessa tali justificatione, a qua non valeant excidere qui praedestinati sunt, non auferri liberrimum arbitrium, sed potius firmius et validius fieri per certitudinem luminis, et per adjectum robur fortitudinis. Unde posse non perseverare in fide, posse deficere a sanctitate, uno verbo, posse peccare et perire, non est libertas, aut pars libertatis, sed liberi arbitrii morbus vel imbecillitas. Cum igitur data voluntate contraria, eademque fortissima et perseverantissima, efficitur ut in actum non possit exire haec imbecillitas, liberum arbitrium non perimitur, sed liberum in bono stabilitur. Tanto enim magis libera est voluntas, quanto magis peccato servire non potest, ut bene Augustinus De praed. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 15. Nihili igitur est Jesuitae argumentum; Decretum Dei antecedens facit ut electi non possint excidere a salute, ergo tollit eorum liberum arbitrium.
pass_a: The hand of God therefore it is, not ours, that we do not depart from God: But the hand of God leads and directs the elect to eternal life with such efficacy, that thence his decree stands most firm; and at the same time with such sweetness and liberty, that thence their choice in the good becomes most free. That these can stand together, Valencia confesses, On 1. q. 23 disp. 1 point 4, where he shows that the most ancient and most learned Scholastics were established in this opinion. Ambrose Catharinus also affirms, such a justification having been granted, from which those who are predestinated cannot fall, that most free choice is not taken away, but rather is made firmer and stronger through certainty of light, and through added strength of fortitude. Whence to be able not to persevere in faith, to be able to fall from holiness, in a word, to be able to sin and perish, is not liberty, or a part of liberty, but a disease or weakness of free choice. Since therefore a contrary will having been given, and the same most strong and most persevering, it is brought about that this weakness cannot go forth into act, free choice is not destroyed, but is established free in the good. For so much the more free is the will, the more it cannot serve sin, as Augustine well On the Predestination of the Saints book 1 chapter 15. Of no account therefore is the Jesuit's argument; The antecedent decree of God makes that the elect cannot fall from salvation, therefore it takes away their free choice.
pass_b: So it is God's hand, not ours, that we do not depart from God. That hand leads the elect to eternal life with such efficacy that his decree stands most firm — and with such sweetness and liberty that their choice in the good becomes most free. Valencia grants both can stand together (In 1. q.23 disp.1 p.4), and notes the oldest, most learned Scholastics held it. Ambrosius Catharinus too: grant a justification from which the predestinated cannot fall, and most free choice is not removed but made firmer and stronger by certainty of light and added fortitude. Ability not to persevere in faith, to fall from holiness — in a word, to sin and perish — is not liberty or part of liberty, but free choice's disease or weakness. When a contrary, strongest, most persevering will is given so that weakness cannot go into act, free choice is not destroyed but established free in the good. The freer the will, the less it can serve sin (Augustine, De praed. Sanct. 1.15). So the Jesuit's argument is worthless: The antecedent decree makes the elect unable to fall from salvation, therefore it takes away their free choice.

lemmas.gloss: God's hand leads firmly and sweetly
Scholastic and Catharinus confirm liberty stands

lemmas.lemma: peccare non est libertas / Nihili Jesuitae
lemmas.gloss: ability to perish is weakness, not liberty
